Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
736 AM EDT Fri Oct 16 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 232 AM EDT Friday...

No significant changes were made with this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 232 AM EDT Friday...

1. A strong storm system will bring widespread rain and gusty 
winds today, followed by much colder weather and mountain snow 
showers on Saturday. 

2. Next week continues to look very quiet with temperatures 
near normal and high confidence of an extended dry period of 
weather.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 232 AM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Low pressure is currently moving through central 
Michigan this morning, spreading rain across southern Ontario and 
into northern/central New York. Much of this rain isn't reaching the 
ground yet per NYS Mesonet observations, but expect it won't take 
much longer for the atmosphere to moisten enough for rain to arrive 
in earnest. This precipitation shield will continue to spread over 
New York and into Vermont early this morning as the low lifts along 
the St Lawrence Valley before shifting eastward just north of the 
international border. There are still some indications that one this 
first round of rain moves through, precipitation will turn more 
showery in nature with some spots getting a bit of a break around 
mid morning. Meanwhile, a 55+ kt 850 mb jet, currently moving into 
the eastern Great Lakes, will also make its way to our area. There's 
still some question how much of this will be able to mix to the 
ground as it will be somewhat coincident with the steadier rain, 
especially in northern New York. However, it will at least allow 
temperatures to surge into the upper 50s/low 60s. Mountain summits 
will be very windy as well, with gusts to 60 mph expected. Gusts 
will also likely be strong in the Champlain Valley and the northern 
slopes of the Greens, due to funneling down the valley and 
downsloping off the higher terrain. The aforementioned dry break 
could coincide with the jet's arrival at these areas, so mixing 
could be better as well. Hence still anticipate gusts up to 40 mph 
in these locations, with perhaps some briefly higher gusts at times. 
This could be enough to bring a few branches down, perhaps resulting 
in isolated power outages, but widespread impacts are not expected 
at this time. Elsewhere, gusts will remain in the 25 to 35 mph 
range. 

The low moves to our north by mid day, dragging its attendant cold 
front across northern New York and Vermont during the afternoon and 
early evening. The latest CAM guidance shows convective showers 
developing ahead of/along this front as it pushes southeastward. 
We'll have little to no instability given the early morning 
rainfall, so anticipate showers won't be organized or strong/severe 
in our area. Still, there may be a few rumbles of thunder, 
especially in southern Vermont. Total rainfall through the daylight 
hours today will be 0.50 to 1.0 inch, with locally higher amounts in 
the higher terrain. 

Winds will turn to the northwest behind the cold front, ushering in 
a much colder airmass. Moisture will linger for a time overnight, 
and the northwest flow will cause showers to focus on the favored 
western upslope sides of the Adirondacks and northern/central 
Greens. Rain will gradually transition to snow as temperatures fall 
overnight. Showers should wane in coverage through the night and 
especially Saturday morning as drier air works in behind a secondary 
front, coming to an end by afternoon. Between the brief timing of 
snow and the relatively warm ground, snow accumulations will be 
minimal and mainly confined to elevations above 1500 ft. Even there, 
accumulations will likely be half inch or less. The highest summits 
could see upwards of 2 inches or so. 

Saturday will be much colder, with highs only in the mid 30s to mid 
40s. Sun should start to break out in the afternoon, but winds will 
remain brisk, with gusts 25 to 30 mph. The morning will start out 
with wind chills in the teens and 20s; the summits will likely feel 
like the single digits in the morning, with negative numbers 
possible. These wind chills improve only slightly through the day, 
so anyone who has outdoor plans should prepare for bitterly cold 
conditions.

KEY MESSAGE 2: South to southwest flow will resume on Sunday, and we 
will moderate closer to seasonal norms with widespread 50s for highs 
under high pressure. This high pressure should shift north and east, 
then to start the work week, another high pressure over Quebec will 
dive southeastward into northern New England and the southern 
Canadian Maritimes, keeping our forecast area dry. Ahead of a weak 
back door cold front, daytime temperatures will be in the upper 50s 
and lower 60s Tuesday, decreasing slightly for the second half of 
the week. Nighttime temperatures next week fall into the mid 20s to 
lower 40s. Fire weather concerns will increase next week due to the 
long duration of dry weather anticipated, but winds will remain 
mostly light and terrain driven under high pressure.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Through 12Z Saturday...
A strong storm system is bringing widespread rain, MVFR 
ceilings, lowered visibilities, low level wind shear, and gusty 
surface winds today, followed by mountain snow showers tonight.

Rain has begun across northern New York and Vermont this
morning, resulting in visibility restrictions of 4-6 miles or
higher, with a few brief periods of 1-3 mile vis in heavier
precipitation. On and off rain showers will continue today, with
lull periods in between. Precipitation will likely come to an
end around 22Z Friday - 00Z Saturday, potentially lingering
later and changing to a rain/snow mix in the mountain sites
(SLK, MPV, EFK) around 02Z-06Z Saturday. Highest confidence of
any snow is at SLK from 03Z-08Z Saturday. 

Lowered ceilings are also in full swing across the forecast area
this morning, with cigs ranging from 300 to 3100 feet above 
ground level. We expect mostly ceilings between 1200-3500 for 
much of today at BTV, PBG, MPV, and RUT. Site MSS has already 
reported steady ceilings 300-500 feet AGL this morning in
northeasterly flow, and we expect IFR or LIFR ceilings to 
persist through around 21Z Friday. Sites SLK and EFK have the 
potential for IFR ceilings as well, most likely between 15Z and 
21Z Friday. Otherwise, sites could see occasional dips into IFR 
cig territory throughout the day today. 

Winds aloft will be strong (30-55 knots) today out of the 
southwest, resulting in periods of LLWS at all sites over the
next 24 hours. Surface winds are also already beginning to mix
down some breezier gusts 15-30 knots out of the south, except at
MSS which has its northeasterly wind 5-10 knots instead. Winds
will continue to be gusty over the next 24 hours, turning more
southwesterly around 15Z-22Z Friday. Highest gusts are expected
in the Champlain Valley 35-40 knots out of the south from 14Z
through 20Z Friday. 


Outlook...

Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Monday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&

.MARINE...
A Lake Wind Advisory remains in effect for Lake Champlain today.
South winds will increase early this morning, becoming 15 to 30
knots with gusts to 35 knots. Locally higher gusts possible.
Winds will turn to the northwest and lessen somewhat after a
cold front moves through later this afternoon, but the Lake
Wind Advisory will likely need to remain in place through
Saturday.

&&
